The causal framing is careful and educational. The discussion of why associational feature importance and perturbation-based pixel explanations can fail is accessible and likely useful to an XAI audience.

Using PAG learning/FCI is a sensible fit for the stated goal, and the simulation provides a clean demonstration that the approach can distinguish a possible causal determinant from a feature associated through an omitted cause under the assumed conditions.
The manuscript is generally well written, transparent about several limitations, and includes appendices with enough preprocessing and implementation detail to understand the experimental pipeline.
weaknesses: The strongest causal language is not fully supported by the empirical evidence. The real-data studies show plausible and interpretable outputs, but they do not validate that the discovered edges correspond to true interventional effects on the black-box models.

The real experiments are fairly weak as evidence: the X-ray study is very small, uses a pneumonia-versus-no-finding control design that may amplify dataset-selection artifacts, and relies on report-mined labels rather than independently validated causal features.

The graph-learning results depend heavily on strong assumptions: faithfulness, adequate conditional independence testing with sparse categorical variables, measurement quality of annotations, and the absence of problematic selection effects. The comparison to LIME and SHAP is mostly qualitative and somewhat asymmetric: those methods answer local pixel-attribution questions, while the proposed method answers a population-level macro-feature causal question. This supports motivation, but not a strong empirical superiority claim.

The simulation is illustrative but highly constructed: the target behavior is partly engineered through shape detectors plus logistic regression, so it does not show that the method will reliably recover causal explanations for more realistic black-box vision systems.

strengths: The paper addresses a real gap in post-hoc explainability: many useful explanations should be stated in terms of macro-level, human-interpretable variables rather than pixels or tokens, and omitted macro variables can induce confounding. This is a useful framing for XAI and causal-discovery audiences.

The conceptual link between interventionist causal explanation, PAGs, and black-box auditing is communicated clearly. The paper is careful in several places to distinguish definite causes, possible causes, and associations attributable to latent confounding.
The Shapley-value example and the synthetic image experiment concretely illustrate why adjustment-based or pixel-level feature attribution can be misleading when relevant macro features are omitted.

The bird and chest-X-ray case studies make the proposed workflow tangible, and the use of bootstrapped graph stability plus a GRaSP-FCI sensitivity analysis gives some evidence that the approach can produce interpretable findings in realistic settings.
The writing is generally self-contained and accessible, with useful background on causal graphs, FCI/PAG interpretation, and limitations around feature construction and measurement error.
weaknesses: The strongest causal claims are only partially supported in the real-data experiments. The applications show clinically or semantically plausible possible causes, but there is no interventional validation, expert adjudication, or external ground truth showing that the learned PAG edges reflect actual causal influence on the model output.

The empirical studies are fairly small and fragile for constraint-based causal discovery. This is especially true for the X-ray study with 240 images, text-mined binary findings, and only 55 test images; chi-square conditional-independence tests and bootstrapped edge frequencies may be unreliable under sparse categorical conditioning.

The synthetic experiment is useful but highly controlled: the black-box model is deliberately constructed so that the final logistic layer depends on selected shape detectors. A broader simulation sweep over graph structures, sample sizes, omitted variables, and discovery hyperparameters would better support robustness claims.

The edge-stability measure is presented as a rough confidence measure, but it is not calibrated and no uncertainty intervals, thresholds, or false-discovery analysis are provided. This limits how actionable the ranked feature lists are.

The comparisons to LIME and SHAP are mostly qualitative and somewhat mismatched, since those methods provide local pixel-level explanations while the proposed method provides population-level macro-feature causal structure. The comparison supports motivation but not a strong empirical superiority claim.

strengths: The paper targets an important and clearly motivated gap in post-hoc explainability: pixel-level attributions are often poorly aligned with the macro-level concepts that users actually want to audit, and unmeasured confounding among such concepts is a real issue.

The causal framing is useful and mostly well communicated. The manuscript explains why PAG/FCI-style causal discovery is relevant when the analyst has only black-box predictions plus interpretable annotations, and it gives a readable account of how edge types should be interpreted.

The toy simulation is a helpful sanity check: by omitting a true explanatory feature, the authors create an unmeasured-confounding setting and show how FCI can distinguish a possible causal determinant from a merely associated feature in that controlled example.

The real-data case studies on bird classification and chest X-rays make the intended workflow concrete, and the discussion is candid about the dependence on interpretable annotations, background knowledge, and causal discovery assumptions.
weaknesses: The main claims are stronger than the evidence supports. Statements such as providing valid causal explanations and distinguishing causal features from confounded associations are only justified asymptotically under strong assumptions; the experiments do not establish that these conditions hold in the real applications.

The real-data experiments lack ground-truth causal validation. Findings such as Wing Shape, Wing Pattern, Atelectasis, Infiltration, and Effusion being likely causes are plausible, but plausibility is not evidence that intervening on those concepts would change the trained model's prediction. No interventional, counterfactual-editing, or held-out causal validation is provided.

The simulation evidence is too narrow. It appears to use a single hand-designed DGP and one omitted-variable scenario, with no systematic evaluation across graph structures, sample sizes, CI-test errors, annotation noise, feature cardinality, or degrees of confounding. This is not enough to support broad methodological claims about reliability.

The finite-sample causal discovery issues are underdeveloped. FCI with chi-square tests, many ordinal variables, capped conditioning sets in the bird experiment, and only 240 X-ray examples can be unstable. Bootstrapped edge frequency is a reasonable heuristic, but it is not calibrated as confidence in causal status, and the bird sensitivity analysis changes the top-ranked features substantially.

The comparison with LIME and SHAP is weak. These methods answer different local attribution questions, are run mostly with default settings, and are assessed qualitatively from a few images. This supports the narrow point that pixel maps can be hard to interpret, but not a strong comparative claim that the proposed approach is empirically superior.

The black-box audit setting is somewhat idealized. The method requires a dataset with reliable macro-level annotations for the same population and enough samples for structure learning; in the X-ray case, the features are text-mined report labels rather than independently validated visual interventions. Measurement error and annotation bias could directly affect the learned graph.

Necessary changes would include narrowing the causal claims or adding stronger validation: multiple simulations with quantitative recovery metrics, sensitivity to FCI assumptions and hyperparameters, uncertainty calibration for edge stability, and some form of interventional or counterfactual-image evaluation. Optional improvements include a fairer comparison to concept-based explanation methods and clearer guidance on when the method should abstain from causal conclusions.

The synthetic example is useful as a proof of concept: by omitting a true determinant, it illustrates how FCI can represent latent confounding and distinguish a possible cause from a merely associated feature in a controlled setting.

The manuscript is generally readable, gives substantial background for non-causal-discovery readers, and is transparent about several limitations, including dependence on annotations, background knowledge, and the difficulty of selecting meaningful macro features.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not convincingly supported. The real-data experiments identify plausible features, but there is no ground-truth validation, interventional test, counterfactual image manipulation, held-out domain shift evaluation, expert evaluation, or quantitative benchmark showing that the discovered PAG edges are actually causal determinants of the model outputs.

The evidence relies heavily on FCI under strong assumptions that are unlikely to hold cleanly in the applications: accurate conditional independence testing, faithfulness, no problematic measurement error in annotations, appropriate handling of mixed ordinal/categorical variables, sufficient sample size, and no selection bias. The real-data conclusions are unstable enough to weaken the claimed utility. In the bird experiment, the GRaSP-FCI sensitivity analysis ranks Crown Color and Size highest rather than the FCI-highlighted Wing Shape and Wing Pattern, but the paper treats this as mostly concordant without a clear criterion for reliability or a principled way to decide which result to trust.

The comparison to LIME and SHAP is not very probative. It compares local pixel-level visualization methods against a population-level macro-variable causal discovery method, largely by qualitative inspection of a few examples. The proposed method depends on manually available, high-quality, causally meaningful macro annotations, but this is precisely the difficult part in many target applications. The simulation is convincing for the central technical point: when an important explanatory feature is omitted, FCI can distinguish a possible causal determinant of the black-box output from a feature associated only through latent confounding, whereas standard feature-attribution intuitions may mislead.

The two image-domain case studies are useful demonstrations rather than overclaimed benchmarks. The bird and X-ray experiments show how the method can produce interpretable, population-level hypotheses, and the bootstrap edge-stability summaries plus GRaSP-FCI sensitivity analysis improve credibility.

The paper is appropriately candid about limitations: dependence on hand-crafted or annotated macro-features, causal discovery assumptions, finite-sample instability, measurement error in annotations, and the role of domain knowledge.
weaknesses: The real-data evidence remains primarily illustrative. For the bird and X-ray experiments, there is no interventional validation or independent expert adjudication that the discovered possible causes are truly causal determinants of the trained model output. The paper should keep causal claims about these applications carefully qualified as hypotheses supported under discovery assumptions.

The X-ray experiment is small and simplified: only 240 images are used, with 55 held out for testing, and the interpretable labels are mined from reports. This limits confidence in the stability and clinical interpretation of the learned PAG, especially given the known difficulty and noise of ChestX-ray8 labels.

The causal discovery pipeline relies on strong assumptions and tuning choices that are not fully stress-tested: faithfulness, reliable chi-square conditional independence tests on coarsened categorical variables, bootstrap interpretation as edge confidence, and a maximum conditioning set size of 4 in the bird experiment. strengths: The paper frames a clear and useful problem: post-hoc explanation of black-box predictors using macro-level, human-interpretable features rather than pixel/token-level perturbations. This is well motivated for auditing settings where only model queries or outputs are available.

The central causal point is convincing: when the explanatory feature set is incomplete, macro-level explanations can face unmeasured confounding, and standard feature-importance or causal-Shapley-style approaches can be misleading. The toy Shapley example and synthetic image experiment make this issue easy to understand.

The proposed use of PAG learning/FCI is technically appropriate for the stated target: distinguishing definite or possible causal ancestors of the model output from features associated through latent common causes. The paper is careful to describe the causal semantics of PAG edge types and the needed background knowledge.

The simulation study provides direct evidence for the main methodological claim in a controlled setting: with an omitted relevant feature, FCI can separate a possible cause of the classifier output from a merely confounded associated feature.

The real-data case studies on bird classification and pneumonia detection are useful demonstrations for the intended audience. They show how the pipeline can produce interpretable, domain-level candidate explanations and how stability over bootstraps can be used as a pragmatic confidence measure.

The writing is generally clear, pedagogical, and accessible to readers from explainable AI who may not already know causal discovery. The limitations section is unusually helpful, especially regarding feature annotation, background knowledge, noisy labels, and the interpretability/data-driven feature tradeoff.
weaknesses: The empirical support for the real-data causal conclusions is limited.
